text: In February, a litre of petrol cost twenty rand ten. By October, it was thirty rand twenty-five. A record.
Here's what happened, month by month, and what it did to everything else you buy.
January to March was calm. Prices hovered around twenty rand, and in February oil was near sixty-six dollars a barrel.
Then, at the end of February, strikes on Iran shook the oil market. By mid-March, Brent crude was above a hundred dollars.
South Africa sets fuel prices on the previous month's costs. So in April, petrol jumped three rand six cents, even after government cut the fuel levy by three rand a litre.
May added another three rand twenty-seven. In June, as the relief began to end, petrol peaked at twenty-eight rand six.
That relief cost the state seventeen point two billion rand. Without it, every litre would have cost even more.
In July and August, oil cooled, and prices eased to twenty-five rand fifty-eight.
But in September, oil climbed back toward a hundred dollars, and the rand stayed weak. October brought the biggest jump of the year: three rand thirty-three, to a record thirty rand twenty-five.
Fuel doesn't stay at the pump. It moves trucks, food, and taxis.

Inflation followed the same road. Three percent in February. Four in April. Five percent in June, the highest in two years. In September it was four and a half, with transport prices up almost eleven percent.
To keep inflation in check, the Reserve Bank raised interest rates in May, and again in September.
Now a new levy cut starts on the fourth of November. One rand fifty off petrol, and three rand off diesel, until December.
Watch the fourth. Fuel moves first. Everything else follows.
